clinicalPearls: Malakoplakia is a rare chronic granulomatous inflammatory condition arising from defective macrophage killing of bacteria, most often coliforms such as Escherichia coli
It most commonly affects the urinary tract, particularly the bladder, but can involve the kidneys, gastrointestinal tract, skin and other organs
It is strongly associated with immunosuppression, chronic infection, malignancy and debilitated states
Cystoscopically it appears as soft yellow-brown mucosal plaques or nodules
The diagnostic histological hallmark is the Michaelis-Gutmann body, a laminated calcified inclusion within large macrophages (von Hansemann cells)
Management combines prolonged antibiotics that concentrate intracellularly, such as fluoroquinolones or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, with reduction of immunosuppression where possible
Surgical excision may be required for large, obstructive or destructive lesions
reference.pathophysiology: Malakoplakia is thought to arise from a defect in the intracellular killing and digestion of phagocytosed bacteria, typically coliform organisms, by macrophages. Incompletely degraded bacterial fragments accumulate within these cells, and mineralisation of the residual material with calcium and iron produces the characteristic laminated Michaelis-Gutmann bodies. The resulting collections of engorged macrophages form the soft plaques and nodules seen clinically. Because the underlying problem is impaired bacterial clearance, the condition is closely linked to immunosuppression and chronic infection, and can produce mass-like or obstructive lesions in affected organs.
additionalDifferentials: Tuberculosis or other chronic granulomatous infection
Other chronic inflammatory or infective plaques
Whipple disease when the gut is involved
additionalInvestigations: Biopsy for histology demonstrating von Hansemann macrophages and Michaelis-Gutmann bodies
Special stains (von Kossa for calcium, Perls for iron, periodic acid-Schiff) to highlight the inclusions
Urine and tissue cultures, commonly yielding coliform organisms
Cystoscopy or endoscopy to characterise mucosal plaques
Cross-sectional imaging to define the extent of organ involvement
Assessment of immune status and screening for underlying malignancy
redFlags: Obstructive uropathy or renal impairment from urinary tract lesions
Mass lesions mimicking or coexisting with malignancy
Systemic infection in an immunosuppressed patient
reference.prognosis: Localised disease often responds to prolonged intracellularly active antibiotics and control of predisposing factors, but extensive or renal involvement, particularly in immunosuppressed patients, carries a worse outlook and may require surgery.
pitfalls: Mistaking mass-forming lesions for malignancy without biopsy
Choosing antibiotics that do not penetrate macrophages well
Overlooking and failing to reduce contributory immunosuppression
Underestimating the risk of urinary obstruction and renal damage
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
